name: Panax ginseng

card.summary: A classic East Asian adaptogen root sold for energy, libido and testosterone; a Cochrane review found small, likely not clinically meaningful effects on erectile function.
card.aka: Korean ginseng, Asian ginseng, red ginseng
card.note: Can interact with drugs such as warfarin; reported side effects include headache, insomnia and raised blood pressure.

quick.overview:
Panax ginseng is a perennial root herb from the Russian Far East, northeast China and Korea, central to traditional East Asian medicine as a tonic. It is processed as white or red ginseng and sold as capsules, extracts and drinks for energy, stress and sexual function.

In men with mild to moderate erectile dysfunction, a Cochrane review of nine placebo-controlled trials (587 men) found small improvements in erectile function that were likely not clinically meaningful, mostly on low-certainty evidence. Wikipedia states there is little evidence of a health effect.
quick.mechanism: The active constituents are thought to be ginsenosides, triterpene saponins that have been studied for effects on inflammation, vascular tone and nitric oxide signaling. Network-pharmacology and laboratory work proposes multiple targets; human mechanistic evidence is limited.
quick.risks: Wikipedia lists headache, raised blood pressure, diarrhea, insomnia and rash as common side effects, notes possible interactions with prescription drugs such as warfarin, and says use in pregnancy and breastfeeding is potentially unsafe.

lead: Panax ginseng, also called Asian, Chinese or Korean ginseng, is a perennial plant native to mountainous areas of the Russian Far East, northeast China and the Korean peninsula; its root is the original source of ginseng and is harvested after five or six years of cultivation [1]. It is used in folk and traditional medicine as a tonic [1][2].

In appearance and fitness communities and the wider supplement market it is sold for energy, stress, libido and testosterone support, and appears in multi-herb men's-health products [3]. Research has examined it for erectile dysfunction, fatigue, cognition and other outcomes. A Cochrane review concluded that effects on erectile function were small and probably not clinically meaningful, with mostly low-certainty evidence [4]. Wikipedia states there is little evidence that it provides any health effect, and that its constituents are under preliminary research [1].

paras: Ginseng root is used in traditional East Asian medicine as a general tonic and is sold as capsules, extracts, teas and drinks. Modern marketing emphasizes fatigue, stress resilience, cognition and sexual function [1][2].

A Cochrane systematic review of nine trials (587 men with mild to moderate erectile dysfunction) compared ginseng only with placebo over up to 12 weeks. Gains in erectile function were small and probably not clinically meaningful; men may report better ability to have intercourse; adverse events did not clearly differ; most evidence was low certainty; and no trial compared ginseng with PDE-5 inhibitors [4]. A 2024 randomized trial of 98 men tested a combination of ginseng, Tribulus terrestris and L-arginine versus placebo and reported improved IIEF-5 scores overall, with no significant benefit in men with diabetes [4].

ClinicalTrials.gov lists ginseng trials on fatigue and stress, cancer-related fatigue, cognition, bone metabolism and exercise-induced muscle soreness [6]. Studies of ginseng on testosterone are discussed in a 2021 systematic review of herbs, which reported some supporting evidence for Asian red ginseng but concluded evidence was limited [7].

Wikipedia reports that ginseng is generally considered safe for adults when used under six months, possibly unsafe longer, and lists headache, raised blood pressure, diarrhea, insomnia, rash and vaginal bleeding as side effects; it may interact with prescription drugs such as warfarin, and its use during pregnancy and breastfeeding is potentially unsafe [1]. Reviews of herb-drug interactions and perioperative care discuss ginseng among herbs that may affect bleeding and blood sugar [8][9].

The main bioactive constituents are ginsenosides, whose chemistry, biosynthesis and proposed effects on inflammation and the vascular system have been reviewed [5][10]. Pharmacology reviews describe multiple constituents with multiple, sometimes opposing, actions [10].

French Jesuit Pierre Jartoux described the plant in a 1711 letter, recording a Chinese name meaning form of man in reference to the root's shape [1]. It is protected in Russia and China, and most commercial supply comes from cultivation [1].
